column2: Jucheng Bank kept a room especially for Yu Si, and he dealt with much of his official business there. Today, however, he was free. Chen Shilong could talk at leisure. He first gave a general account of Hu Xueyan's affairs in Shanghai and Hangzhou, then came to his need for funds. Yu and Hu already had an arrangement: Fukang lent out Yu's money and paid him half the interest charged to its borrowers—a cost lower even than the interbank rate—and naturally no security was required. Yu called in Jucheng's manager. On learning that thirty thousand taels could be made available, he instructed him to remit the money to Fukang in Hangzhou immediately.

Their business concluded, Chen turned to his private affairs and recounted, from the beginning, Hu's intentions and arrangements concerning A’zhu. Yu found it more entertaining than a storyteller's performance. He listened on the opium couch, continued listening at the dining table, and returned to the couch for more. When Chen finished, he said, “You have to admire Old Hu! The things he does are so original, and so beautifully managed.” “Uncle Four, the wedding should be towards the end of the year. When we send out invitations, I'll need you to represent me.” “Naturally!” He gave a long sigh. “Things have turned out well for you...” The occasion had evidently brought A’hu to mind. Chen hastened to say, “Don't grieve, Uncle Four. A’hu is gone, but I'm still here to look after you.” Yu's eyes reddened. Whether from grief for his son or gratitude to Chen, it was hard to tell. At last he forced himself to rally. “Little Monk, you know I've wronged you in some ways. That's past, and we needn't say more. Now you're establishing a home and a livelihood and taking the proper road. I'm delighted. Of course I'll represent you in the marriage, and I'll take responsibility for everything. Find out how much Old Hu paid for those four kinds of jewellery. I'll repay him. With me here, he ought not to pay for your betrothal gifts.”

Naturally Chen was grateful. Yet, brief as his time with Hu had been, his intelligence, adaptability, and wholehearted willingness to learn had greatly advanced his understanding of the world. He had sincerely meant to comfort an elder; now Yu was treating him as family. That was good in itself. But trouble would come sooner or later within Yu's household, and Sister A’lan was already scheming about her parents' property. If he accepted benefits now, people might think he too was taking advantage of Yu's vulnerability. He must avoid that suspicion. Even that was a lesser concern. A’lan appeared to be managing Yu's household now. The four kinds of jewellery would cost a thousand taels; if Yu paid that sum back to Hu, A’lan would be displeased as soon as she heard, and there would be no end of talk. “Well?” Yu was puzzled by his silence. “What is there to say about it?” Chen had decided to decline but could not find the words. Pressed, he answered, “Uncle Four, it isn't that I fail to appreciate your kindness. I want to prove myself and manage this myself. Ultimately, that will do you credit too. You'll be able to tell people that Little Monk paid for his own marriage. You offered to provide the betrothal gifts, but he didn't need it. Won't that give you something to be proud of?”

In their world, standing mattered, and so did the saying that a man should support himself. An elder could hardly withhold approval. “I'm pleased to hear you say that. But...” Yu's tone became admonitory. “You're only just starting out. Don't learn to boast before you learn anything else. That wouldn't do.” “I'm speaking honestly. What would be the point of boasting, especially before you?” “Then let me ask you seriously: where will you get the money to marry? Didn't you say Old Hu bought the jewellery for you?” “Yes. Mr Hu advanced the money. I can repay him from my share of the profits later. If you provided the money, wouldn't you scold me when I tried to pay you back?” “It's all the same. When you have money, you can show your respect for me too.” “Of course! If I don't honour you with it, whom should I spend it on? For now, though, please help me keep my pride and prove myself. Let me manage everything.” Yu was both pleased and perplexed. The first part delighted him: even if it was flattery, it felt good. The second troubled him. Leaving Chen to his own devices would help him prove himself and preserve his standing; paying for his wedding would apparently do the opposite! What sort of reasoning was that?

Unreasonable though it sounded, Yu could not refute it. Leaning back, he studied Chen and pointed at him with the opium needle. “I haven't seen you for two or three months, and you've changed! In that long gown, you look quite like a senior business clerk. And the things you say are so extraordinary that they're harder to answer than an official pronouncement from above. Did you learn all this from Old Hu?” He sounded regretful but was secretly delighted. Chen merely smiled, then stood. “Uncle Four, I have several matters to attend to. I'll come and see you again tomorrow.” “Come to my house tomorrow—the North Gate house.” Yu made the address quite clear, then sighed again. “These days have been unbearable. Seeing you today has made me feel much better. If you're free tonight, do come again. I have more to tell you. If you can't come tonight, you must come tomorrow morning. I seldom go to the tea shop now. I went today only to wait for you. Otherwise I'd have stayed brooding at home. I even think of giving up my post at the yamen. There's no point!” He shook his head repeatedly. That Yu could contemplate abandoning even his hereditary position showed how despondent he had become. Chen felt sorry for him and wanted to stay, entertaining him with interesting stories of the foreign settlement. But the day had already been delayed too long, beginning with Crystal A’qi's visit. He had to leave and attend to business.

By the time he completed his rounds and finished the tasks Hu had entrusted to him, the evening light was fading. He hurried to Dajing Silk Firm, where Huang Yi came forward to greet him. “Your mother-in-law has just left. She made up your room and waited quite a while, but when you didn't come, she had to go home. Before leaving, she told me over and over to send you there for supper. Nobody could fault the way she treats her son-in-law!” “I've been anxious too.” Chen felt uneasy. “I simply couldn't get away. Even now I can't go immediately. I want to write to Mr Hu first and send the letter on the regular boat as soon as possible.” “You can write when you come back tonight. You're staying here anyway.” “No!” Living at Dajing seemed to Chen much like marrying into his wife's household. A man with backbone would not live as a dependent son-in-law in his wife's family home. He therefore said firmly, “I'm still staying at my own place.” Huang understood. “That's up to you. But I'd advise you to go to the Zhangs soon. You can write the letter there just as well.”

Chen accepted that suggestion. When he reached the Zhang house, A’zhu herself opened the door. This time she was not as embarrassed as she had been the day before. “Why have you come so late?” she asked with a trace of reproach. “Several unexpected things happened. Ah!” He shook his head. “Sighing as soon as you come in! Why?” She was deeply concerned. “It isn't anything that's happened to me,” he said first, lest she misunderstand and worry. “A close friend has died unexpectedly. Truly, storms come without warning, and a person's fortune can change overnight.” His unhappy expression saddened her too. Closing the front gate, she led him into the sitting room. “Father has gone to a wedding feast, so there's nobody to keep you company. Would you like to come into the kitchen?” “Certainly. I'll greet your mother there, then find a moment to write to Mr Hu.” The greeting took a long time. As she cooked, A’zhu's mother asked question after question about what Chen had done that day. Once they began discussing A’hu, there was no end to it. Naturally, he said nothing whatever about Crystal A’qi. “Well,” A’zhu said with a smile when the meal was ready, “you haven't managed to write your letter after all.” “I'll write after supper. It must be done today.”

This was proper business, and A’zhu's mother regarded it as important. After the meal, she hurried to clear the table, make tea, and set out brush and inkstone. A’zhu spread the paper and ground the ink for him. Even Chen felt that they were making too much of it. “This looks less like a letter than a memorial to the emperor,” he said with a self-mocking smile. “Less chatter! Finish it quickly and take it to the boat. If they've gone to sleep, you'll have to get up very early tomorrow to catch them.” Tomorrow would have its own business. Determined to repay kindness through diligent work, Chen held to the rule of finishing today's tasks today. He collected his thoughts and reported, item by item, how he had carried out Hu's instructions. At the end, he mentioned Yu: his only son's death, the threatened family troubles, and his low spirits. Naturally, Chen included news of his own marriage arrangements. When he finished and looked at the clock, it had already struck nine. He hurriedly took his leave and delivered the letter himself to the boat bound for Hangzhou, then went straight home.

Before he reached his door, he noticed something strange. There was light inside—and more than one lamp was burning. Chen never locked his door when he went out. There was nothing worth stealing, and forgetting or losing a key would be a nuisance. Besides, neighbours who shared the entrance could keep an eye on the place. Sometimes a visiting friend, finding him absent, would push open the door and sit down to wait. But that happened by day. This was the first such occasion at night, and it surprised and intrigued him. Who could it be? Instead of entering directly, he crept beneath the window and peered through a hole in the paper. One look told him he was in serious trouble. Crystal A’qi sat drinking tea by a lamp polished bright, her eyes fixed on another lamp across the room, as though turning over countless worries. She wore a purplish-red, lined jacket of Ning silk. Its collar was unfastened and spread wide, revealing glimpses of the gold chain that held her underbodice. Anyone seeing her like this would certainly say that Crystal A’qi and Little Monk were having an affair. Furious, Chen went to the door and raised his foot to kick it. At that instant, he checked himself. Wait! Who knew what she intended? Her heart was not bad, but her former occupation had stripped away her inhibitions, and she could be as wilful and defiant as anyone. Perhaps, having failed by persuasion, she deliberately meant to provoke a quarrel. If word reached A’zhu, there would be trouble enough. Should the engagement break off, A’qi would have got just what she wanted. Chen felt that this suspicion was mean-minded. Yet he remembered Huang's saying: never intend harm, but never fail to guard against it. He must be cautious with someone like A’qi. Her presence here already showed what he had failed to foresee.

Once he had thought it through, his anger subsided. He pushed open the door. Apparently taken by surprise, A’qi sprang up with wide eyes. Seeing Chen, she patted her chest. “Oh! You frightened me!” “What about the fright you gave me?” he answered calmly. “Don't you look like a fox spirit appearing in the middle of the night?” “Scold away!” She smiled untroubled. “At least I know I haven't come to bewitch you.” “Then what have you come for?” “I thought your bachelor's life looked pitiful. With nothing else to do, I came to tidy this kennel of yours. Surely there's no law against that?” Only then did Chen look round. The room had been put in order. The bed particularly caught his eye: it hardly seemed his own. He never folded his bedding, and with it folded now, the bed looked much larger. “You've gone to a great deal of trouble.” He sat down. “Freshly made tea.” She poured him a cup. “I've a pot of duck congee simmering for you on the veranda.” “Where did the stove and pot come from?” “I bought them.” She counted on her fingers. “A portable stove, teapot, earthenware pot, and charcoal: two thousand copper cash altogether.”

“What else did you buy for me? How much have you spent in all?” “Do you mean to pay me back?” “Naturally. We aren't setting up house together. There's no reason for you to buy these things.” His manner was calm, but there was no warmth in his words. A’qi reproached herself inwardly. Why come here to be snubbed? Yet she could not bear simply to leave. Living respectably was one thing; enduring desolation and loneliness was another. Alone beside a lamp on an autumn night of cold rain, she could bite her quilt to pieces and gain nothing. Better to stay here. Chen might show her no kindness, but at least there were two of them! With this resolution, she gained the advantage. Chen had hoped that embarrassment would send her home. He had never imagined that she might feel unwelcome and stay anyway. Not knowing this, he continued to meet every remark with an uncompromising rejoinder.

A’qi went about her business. She brought in the pot of congee, set it on the floor, and hurried out again. Clattering sounds followed. Unable to imagine what she was doing, Chen went to look and discovered a little kitchen installed round the corner of the veranda: a plain wooden table and a bamboo cupboard against the wall. The noise came from her taking out bowls and chopsticks. She really seemed intent on setting up house with him! He was both annoyed and amused but could say nothing. Returning to his seat, he was followed by A’qi with a tray. Besides two sets of bowls and chopsticks, it held two side dishes: tudie preserved in wine lees, and radish pickled in sauce. “I don't want any,” he said, determined to keep her at a distance. “Then I'll eat!” she answered briskly. She served herself congee and sat down. Whether she was truly hungry or meant to annoy him, she ate with noisy relish. The congee had simmered to perfection, and its rich aroma drifted continually towards him. Watching her bite into crisp pickled radish with an audible crunch made him swallow with longing.

He began to feel aggrieved. “You've made yourself comfortable! Do you really think this is your home?” “We're friends, aren't we?” she answered without concern. “Wouldn't you do the same at my place?” “I wouldn't be so insensitive.” “You mean I'm insensitive?” “A little. It's late. I want to go to bed.” “Little Monk, you're terribly small-minded,” she said quietly. “You could at least let me finish this bowl before driving me away.” The rebuke struck home. Chen regretted his words. He was a grown man; low as his standing in their world might be, nobody had ever dared openly slight him. Yet today her two remarks had put him completely in the wrong. He must recover his ground. “Small-minded? That has nothing to do with it! I'm thinking of you, not driving you away. Stay as long as you please. I don't mind. But you'll have to excuse me.”

He took off his long gown, laid it across a chair, and sat on the edge of the bed to change into slippers. The slippers he had worn that morning were no longer underneath it. A’qi must have moved them. Unwilling to speak to her, he kicked off his shoes and flung himself onto the bed. “Your slippers are here.” She drew them from beneath a square stool at the head of the bed, then hung his gown on the clothes stand and cleared the table. Chen watched in silence, but could not lie comfortably. He felt as though a thorn were sticking into his back. His only wish was that she would leave soon and never return. When she had finished, she sat down. “Little Monk, there's something I want to ask you.” Too embarrassed to ignore her, he answered coldly, “Go ahead.” “Honestly, I've never made such well-flavoured duck congee. Won't you have a bowl?” He had never expected that. Nobody's heart was made of stone. She had worked hard to prepare it, and now must beg him to enjoy it, as though eating a bowl would do her some great favour. He could not bring himself to refuse harshly. “You've cleared everything away. Why go to more trouble...?”

Before he could finish, she was on her feet. “No trouble at all!” She hurried out, and he could not stop her. Chen felt an indescribable vexation with himself. How useless he was, unable even to deal with A’qi! Sitting up, he argued inwardly with his own weakness. Why fear her like a poisonous snake? The more he avoided her, the more tightly she would cling. When she brought the congee with a smile, he offered no thanks, merely took his chopsticks and began to eat, crunching the radish as loudly as she had. He finished one bowl, then had another. “Tastes good, doesn't it?” she asked proudly. “Nothing remarkable.” “Hmph!” She curled her lip at his insincerity. “My congee may be poor, but your appetite seems good.” “My appetite is poor, but you wouldn't be happy if I didn't eat.” Chen imitated her phrasing. A’qi said nothing, quietly savouring his words.

“Now it's my turn to ask a question.” Chen set down his empty bowl. “What exactly do you want from me?” “Nothing much. Honestly, there's nothing for me to do at home. I lie alone in bed, thinking of everything, unable to sleep till morning. Talking to you makes me feel better. When it's time, you can go to bed and I'll go home.” It was a modest request, and Chen's view of her had changed since he came in. He nodded. “Very well. At worst, I'll sit with you till dawn.” She smiled, cleared away the bowls, and made fresh tea. Across the newly brightened lamp, they chatted, though she did most of the talking. Yu Si, she said, was fairly decent in his dealings with people, but too easily influenced, especially by his daughter. She had truly meant to spend her life with him. Who could have foreseen this change? People called women of her former profession low and contemptible, she complained, but knew nothing of how hard it was to leave that life. At this point, the talk became serious. “Little Monk, I made inquiries this afternoon. Your engagement to the Zhang girl is real. I'm a step too late. Then tell me, how am I to live from now on?” Her request for advice was sincere, and Chen could not evade it. After thinking, he replied, “You must first say what you want, so that others can look for you. Could you endure hardship? Would you accept being a concubine? What sort of man do you want? Make it clear, and I'll look. Such a matter can be very difficult or very easy. Mr Hu has arranged three matches in the past two or three months. He's as resourceful at it as at business. I'll entrust your case to him and guarantee good news within three months.”

A’qi merely blinked, as though she herself could not decide what sort of respectable man she should settle with. “Marriage can't be rushed,” Chen said, seizing the chance to encourage her departure. “Go home and think it over. You've suffered once. You mustn't suffer twice.” His earnest tone persuaded her, and she rose as though to leave. Chen moved quickly. He took down the lantern he had brought from Dajing, which hung on a nail in a post, lit its candle, and placed it in her hand. “Then I'll see you tomorrow!” she said. “Tomorrow, tomorrow!” An idea struck him, and he laid the groundwork. “Though you may find it hard to catch me these next two days.” “Why? Are you that busy?” “Yes. You may not believe it, but I even have business from the prefectural yamen to attend to.” There was nothing unbelievable about that. A’qi knew Hu and Prefect Wang were inseparable. As Hu's trusted man, Chen might naturally handle some official matters as well. But official business was done by day, and he must return home to sleep at night. She need not fear being unable to find him.

Night was precisely when Chen wanted to avoid her. As matters stood, sternness would not frighten her away, and he could not outlast her gentle persistence. Of all strategies, retreat was best. He could not leave Huzhou, so there were two possibilities: find another house, or move into Dajing. On reflection, only the second would do. If he found a new place, he would have to explain himself when people asked. Saying he wished to avoid A’qi would look like a guilty conscience and make an innocent matter seem suspicious. Besides, she might call at Dajing. If he lived there, he could handle her more easily. Otherwise, a few careless words from her could arouse suspicions that even the Yellow River could not wash away. His mind settled, he slept peacefully. Early next morning he went to see several younger friends he knew well. Their drinking lasted until three in the afternoon. Then he went home, packed his clothes, and took them to Dajing.

“Come along!” Huang hurried from his room, beckoning. “Your matchmaker has something to tell you today.” Once inside, Chen heard a wholly unexpected story. That morning Yu had come to Dajing especially to see Old Zhang, addressing him as his fellow parent-in-law. Chen, he explained, was his junior, but he now regarded him as a son. At the wedding, Yu would head the bridegroom's family. He had also brought a thousand taels in betrothal money. “Your father-in-law is an honest fellow and didn't know what to do. He came to ask me. What was there to discuss? I told him to acknowledge the relationship.” Huang was delighted. “That's a man of standing for you! He does things magnificently. He gave me two hundred taels as thanks for arranging the match. Refusing would have offended him, so I frankly accepted. I've benefited through you, my young friend.” Chen felt greatly honoured and was very pleased, but hid it lest Huang discover that he had known nothing of the arrangement. “This makes the timing terribly tight,” Huang continued. “Your mother-in-law invited me to lunch and told me she needs at least six months to prepare her daughter's dowry. There isn't time before the year's end. What do you think? Let's settle it between ourselves, then speak to Uncle Four.”

Chen was reluctant. After some thought, he asked, “What does A’zhu say?” “What an unreasonable question! What could she say? That the sooner she leaves home to marry, the better?” Seeing the point, Chen laughed. “I can't decide this. I must discuss it with Uncle Four and Mr Hu.” “Can't you decide your own affairs?” Having accepted Yu's money and the Zhangs' hospitality, Huang had to understand the situation. “Frankly, both your parents are dead. Others may help, but their wishes aren't your parents' commands.” Chen had heard the saying about parental commands and a matchmaker's words. Yet his own marriage was like water whose warmth only the drinker knew. Establishing a home and establishing a livelihood were two sides of the same matter. Hu had arranged the match both to advance Chen and to secure an able assistant for his own enterprises. All those ventures were now being actively developed, and only Hu knew when Chen would be needed. If he were busy with a wedding precisely when his help was required, business would suffer. That could not be Hu's intention. Besides, Chen felt grateful. Only after following Hu and calling him “sir” had he understood how a teacher could truly be like a father. Out of respect, he would willingly seek Hu's approval even without any risk of disrupting business. Seeing him silent in thought, Huang understood that he had difficulties. But the bride's family had difficulties too, and Chen must first understand them. Otherwise, carrying messages between two sides pulling in opposite directions would be thankless work.

“Shilong,” Huang said persuasively, “a person has only one wedding night, and she's her family's only daughter. If preparing her dowry delays the wedding, we on the bridegroom's side must be considerate. Great families begin preparing a daughter's dowry when she's twelve or thirteen. Taking five or six years is nothing unusual. Here they ask for only five or six months. That's not much. Tell Mr Hu. He understands human affairs thoroughly and will certainly agree.” “I know he's very likely to agree. But I must tell him first.” “Then that's settled.” Huang pointed to Chen's bundle of clothes. “You've changed your mind? You think it would be more convenient to stay here after all?” An idea struck Chen. He could not tell other people about A’qi, but the matchmaker was precisely the person who should know. If a misunderstanding arose later, he would have an influential witness. He sighed. “I've come to take refuge!” “Why?” Huang was both surprised and concerned. “What trouble prevents you from staying in your own home? Do you owe someone money?” “A debt, yes, but not a money debt...”

After hearing the story, Huang laughed. “A debt of love, indeed! Shilong, fortune certainly favours you with women.” His tone turned envious. “Young fellows know how to manage these things!” “And you still tease me! Nobody else knows about this. Mr Huang, you must help.” “You've acted correctly and kept your footing. Don't worry!” Huang struck his chest. “As long as you hold firm and resist her temptation, leave everything to me. If she comes here, I've a splendid plan for dealing with her. I guarantee you won't have the least trouble.” Such confidence aroused Chen's curiosity as well as his interest. Smiling, he asked, “Could you tell me this wonderful plan beforehand?” “Heaven's secrets mustn't be revealed!” Huang paused to consider, then asked suddenly, “One more thing. Are you absolutely certain she and Uncle Four parted amicably? They didn't quarrel?” “So it appears. Otherwise Uncle Four isn't easy to deal with either.” “When she comes, hide yourself. Whatever happens, don't appear. I have my own way of driving off the enemy.”

Chen had no idea what Huang was planning. Still, with this shield in place, he could feel at ease. He moved into the bedroom his mother-in-law had prepared, slept briefly, then went out again to thank Yu and keep him company for a while. Afterwards he visited the Zhangs. A’zhu's mother was warmer towards him than ever, yet also seemed more formal. “I've moved into the firm,” he told her, without giving any reason. “As you should.” Naturally she was pleased. “Come home for your meals every day. The food at the firm is quite good, but it can't be as comfortable as eating at home.” While they talked, A’zhu remained in her room. She had many questions for Chen, but felt increasingly shy. He felt the same. Unable to intrude, he kept looking towards the lamp and dark silhouette behind her white paper window. At last, with nothing more to say, he rose to leave. Her mother neither detained him nor mentioned A’zhu, and he departed disconsolately. As he walked, he wondered whether his mother-in-law meant to keep them apart. Why would she? It was puzzling. Naturally, he did not want to suspect anything bad, yet could hardly call it a good sign. He could only reassure himself that it was an isolated occurrence.

Next morning he rose clear-headed, able to think sharply and thoroughly. He must find useful work in Huzhou. If there was none, he should return to Hangzhou and ask for Hu's instructions. Idling in comfort was no sound policy. Reviewing the situation, he found something he could do: investigate silk prices. Hu urgently wanted this information and had been making inquiries in Hangzhou. But most silk intended for export came from Huzhou, and reports gathered elsewhere might be inaccurate. With nothing else to do, Chen could help him directly. Then he reconsidered. Huang knew that business well. If prices changed, he would surely write to Hu. Why duplicate the work? Better to call on the two advisers at the county yamen and inquire about official developments. If all was quiet, he might as well return to Hangzhou. The visit came to nothing; indeed, it was a rebuff. Access to the quarters of the legal and financial advisers was strictly controlled, and casual visitors were never allowed to wander in. Chen did not know Yang Yongzhi and the other adviser well. When he sent his name through their attendants, both refused to receive him. He was displeased, but admitted that he had been presumptuous and had learned another lesson. Back at Dajing, he sat about bored and decided to visit his own rooms. He had barely stepped out when an apprentice hurried up with Huang's message: he must leave by the back door immediately.

A’qi had come looking for him. Curiosity made Chen unwilling to leave. “Has a lady come to see Mr Huang?” “Yes.” “What did he say to her?” “He smiled and invited her inside, calling her Sister A’qi.” Chen decided to investigate. Dismissing the apprentice, he slipped through a side door towards Huang's room. Beside it was a staircase, with a locked storeroom beneath. Chen quietly unlocked it and hid there to listen. “Sister A’qi,” he heard Huang say, “I didn't know you were acquainted with Shilong.” “We've known each other for years.” “Then you're old sweethearts?” Huang's bluntness bordered on rudeness, and Chen frowned. Just then, a ray of light entered through the partition. There was a hole which Huang's back had previously blocked. He had changed seats, letting the light through. Guided by it, Chen moved silently and put his eye to the opening. Both were in view. A’qi was plainly dressed in a lightly padded jacket of iron-grey xianchun fabric and a black skirt of imported crepe. She wore no rouge or powder, only a red flower at her temple. The effect was both dignified and pretty, with the captivating charm of a mature woman. Her expression was dignified too, provided her eyes remained still. Once they moved, they glittered like sunlight on water, dazzling the observer. Absorbed in looking, Chen forgot to listen and missed whatever had been said in the interval. A’qi now looked slightly angry. Huang must have been speaking too discourteously.

“Sister A’qi,” Huang was saying, “if your relationship is entirely proper and there's nothing between you, why have you come to see Shilong?” “I entrusted a small sum to him to lend at interest. Now I need money and want him to call it back.” Chen was first astonished, then angry. Wasn't this a false accusation? She had never given him money to lend. A little thought made her purpose clear: she was smoking a rat out of its hole. She meant to force him to appear. It was a brilliant scheme, and he feared Huang would be unable to answer it. But Huang understood. Chen had told him about her relations with Yu. Previously, Chen had scarcely been able to meet her, so how could he have handled her money? Besides, Yu owned Jucheng with partners. If A’qi had savings, why not deposit them there for interest instead of asking Chen to lend them? Knowing she was lying, Huang chose not to expose her. “How much is it, and how much do you need back?” “Not much. A few hundred taels. As much as he can recover.” “Very well. I'll tell him.”

“Thank you.” After a pause, A’qi continued, “But I'd like to settle the account with him personally. When should I come to find him?” “To tell you the truth, you won't find him at any time.” “Why?” “Because seeing you would bewitch him, and I have a responsibility.” The force lay in its unexpectedness. Like a thunderclap, it shattered her carefully calculated plan to draw Chen out step by step, leaving her bewildered and discouraged. Huang was smiling as though he meant mischief. Resenting him, A’qi straightened her back and thrust out her full bosom. “Never mind whether he's bewitched. I'd like to ask what you mean by responsibility. I want to discuss proper business with Chen Shilong. Why are you obstructing me?” “He's engaged to be married. I arranged the match and am responsible to the bride's family. If the bridegroom sees you, loses his head, and does something foolish, they'll come to me. What could I tell them?” Huang changed seats again, moving to a lower chair beside her and leaning towards her across the tea table. “Think about it, Sister A’qi. Isn't that reasonable?” Her face whitened with anger. “Very reasonable!” she answered with repeated cold laughs. Watching, Chen was amused but also sorry for her. If Huang meant to anger her into leaving, it was a poor plan. Chen knew her temper: kindness persuaded her, force did not. Resentment could provoke any sort of outrageous scene. Wouldn't that make matters worse?

While Chen was beginning to regret the arrangement, Huang changed his expression. All apology and caution, he said humbly, “Sister A’qi, I've offended you. You're angry with me, aren't you?” “Hmph!” She smiled coldly. “How would I dare be angry with you?” “Oh dear!” Huang scratched his head, looking desperately troubled. “That sounds very angry indeed. I apologise. Please don't be offended.” This made her uncomfortable, and she softened. “I'm not angry. Why should I be?” “Truly?” His tone became playful. “If you aren't angry, give me a smile.” How could she? He was proving difficult to handle. Looking closely, she saw his lustful eyes fixed on her breast and suddenly understood. So that was what he wanted! Recalling his offensiveness, she resolved to teach him a lesson. The anticipated pleasure of revenge brightened her mood. She smiled, her eyes sparkling, then rose and walked a few steps before turning to glance sideways at him, as though about to speak. Her lowered gaze and seductive movements were artful indeed. Huang felt as though seventeen or eighteen little hands were tickling his heart. His plan had been to offer himself in Chen's place, rescuing the young man and gaining an advantage for himself. He had begun by deliberately offending her, to end her hopes of Chen, then intended to win her over through the deference prescribed in the old seducer's formula of looks, virility, wealth, humility, and leisure. He had expected this to require considerable effort. Such swift success delighted him beyond expectation.

“Sister A’qi,” he began insinuatingly, “Shilong told me you're alone and very lonely. Is that true?” “Yes.” She looked elsewhere, seemingly too shy to meet his eyes. “Otherwise I wouldn't have come looking for him.” “Finding him won't help now. Chen Shilong forgets old affections for new ones. His whole heart is set on Miss Zhu of the Zhang family.” Jealousy stirred again. “Hmph! I've seen A’zhu. Even a mere slip of a girl gets called ‘Miss’ now. What a world!” “Let's leave that. It only makes you unhappy. Tell me, Sister A’qi, where do you live?” “Where Old Yu used to live. I'm alone there now.” “No wonder! Living alone is too lonely. Why not hire a maid for company?” “I have one. As stupid as an ox and as dull as a pig. After supper she starts dozing, and once in bed she's like a dead person.”

“Then your nights must be lonely. Doesn't anyone come to see you?” “Who would? Not even a ghost crosses my threshold.” “Then,” Huang asked with an ingratiating smile, “may I be the ghost?” “What sort of talk is that?” “You said not even a ghost comes. I'll be the ghost at your door!” “Oh!” Folding her arms across her chest, A’qi pretended to shudder. “Come if you like! Why talk of ghosts at the door? You make it sound frightening.” Her manner was affected but charming. Huang particularly relished her first words, taking them as an unguarded revelation of her true feelings. Once he could visit her house, with a woman of her background, he felt sure of being admitted to her bed.

The thought made his hands less restrained. “Don't be frightened. We're only joking.” He took her hand quite naturally. She gazed at him with a smile, as though enjoying some secret thought. Suddenly she snatched her hand away and said sternly, “Keep your hands to yourself!” As she spoke, she glanced behind her. Huang thought he understood again: touching was acceptable; being seen was the danger. That was easy to remedy. “What's going on? I sent the apprentice to buy refreshments, and he still hasn't returned!” Muttering this, he hurried outside. In the adjoining space, Chen was puzzled. What did A’qi mean? Could loneliness truly have made her willing to accept Huang's advances? He tried to study her expression, but her back was turned as she looked out of the window. Then came Huang's footsteps, followed by the sound of a door closing and a bolt sliding home. So that was it! Huang was far too impatient. There would certainly be a performance worth watching from next door.

“What do you think of my room?” Huang returned smiling. “Once the door is shut, not even a fly can get in.” “I understand!” A’qi nodded slowly, pointing at him with an index finger whose nail was stained red with balsam. “You're wicked!” “Wicked? How?” “Ask yourself!” “I don't know.” He took her hand again and smiled ingratiatingly. “Tell me.” “Why should I?” She looked away. “Saying it aloud would spoil it.” “Exactly. No need to say it. Understanding is enough.” As he spoke, he leaned close and inhaled her scent. She tilted her face aside, but with both hands held, she could not move far enough to avoid him. “How fragrant!” Tilting back his head and closing his eyes, Huang sniffed the air twice. Meanwhile, one hand began moving slowly up her arm.

While Huang remained entranced, Chen began to worry for him. A’qi's expression was changing: her eyes widened, her brows rose, and her mouth tightened. At last she raised her fleshy hand and struck him hard across the face. “Ah!” Huang shouted. Opening his eyes and seeing her expression, he finally understood. “Why did you hit me?” he demanded, holding his cheek. “For molesting a respectable woman,” she replied calmly. “You!” He roared and stamped. “You filthy whore...” Before he finished, another slap struck his face. Now A’qi showed her fierce spirit. She darted to the table, snatched up a pair of scissors, and raised them. Through clenched teeth she said, “Use that filthy language again, and I'll jab out your eyes!” Chen was alarmed. Someone might be killed! Fortunately, Huang knew when to retreat. With an embarrassed smile, he said, “Why take it so seriously? If I'd known you couldn't take a joke, I'd have been a damned fool to bother you.” “Hmph!” A’qi threw the scissors onto the table and commanded with a stern face, “Go and open the door. I'm leaving.”

Without a word, Huang obediently opened the door and let her go. Now Chen suffered: it took every ounce of strength to suppress his laughter. Only after Huang had gone well away did he slip out, covering his mouth, and hurry to the neglected garden behind the building. There he clutched his stomach and laughed aloud. In the old days, he would certainly have spread this story at Huang's expense. But he had learned much about human relations from Hu and understood that Huang would desperately want to conceal it. Not only must he keep it to himself; he should preferably pretend ignorance even before Huang. Otherwise he would earn his resentment. This was precisely what the saying meant: trouble comes from talking too much. Yet his problem remained. A’qi would still come. With a nickname like Crystal, she seemed transparent through and through, as though she had no hidden designs. Yet she had proved remarkably skilful at troublesome tricks. Her plan to smoke him out of his hole was formidable and could not be ignored. He must consult Huang again. Taking particular care that his face betrayed nothing, and allowing time for Huang's feelings to settle, he did not seek him immediately. He left by the back door, found a friend to dine with, and only after returning to the firm strolled over to inquire about the news.

“Well?” he asked as though nothing had happened. “How did you get her to leave?” “I told her I'd arranged your match with A’zhu and had a responsibility. I advised her not to trouble you again.” “What did she say?” “A thoroughly bad woman!” Huang said bitterly. “She claimed she'd entrusted savings to you to lend at interest. She wanted her principal back and thought it best to see you. In short, to put it briefly—she's a cheap creature who can't live without a man!” Listening, Chen recalled how Huang had roared like a tiger and ended like a beaten stray. The contrast with his present words made laughter rise irresistibly in his belly. He almost let it escape. “It's become a real problem,” Huang continued more calmly, showing that he had considered it. “Hiding won't be enough now.” “Why?” “If she comes here, I can keep her away. The danger is that she stops coming and spreads rumours everywhere: you owe her money and refuse to see her. Then you'll have to appear and argue with her.” Huang looked up. “Isn't she a bad woman?” Chen did not think her character quite so bad. But if she persisted and he continually avoided her, resentment might build. Then, with a woman like her, who could say? He drew a breath and rubbed his hands uneasily. “Don't let her ruin a good marriage,” Huang warned. “She's leaving you nowhere to turn. You must find a solution soon.”

“Yes. Isn't that why I'm asking your advice?” Huang nodded. His eyes suddenly grew intent, and he considered for some time before speaking slowly. “There is one way. ‘A small-minded man is no gentleman; a man without ruthlessness is no man.’ If you want to settle it once and for all, this is the only road.” It sounded like an exceptionally cruel measure. Chen urged him to explain. “What road, Mr Huang?” “I hear you know the county yamen's legal adviser well?” “Not very well. But with Mr Hu's name behind me, I can obtain a hearing.” “Then it's simple!” Huang sounded quite relaxed. “A’qi isn't a local. Her native place is Gaoyou. Ask the legal adviser to get a warrant issued, have her charged as an itinerant prostitute, and send her under escort back to her home district. Pack her off, damn her!”

Chen had never expected such a plan. It was far too vicious, and he was inwardly shocked. So this was the sort of man Huang was! He would have to be careful in their future dealings. “Well?” Huang pressed. “I'm thinking of you. Nothing less will make you safe.” “Yes, yes. I know you're doing it entirely for me. But...” Chen was quick-witted too and shifted the difficulty onto Yu. “There's Uncle Four to consider. People won't know we're responsible. They'll think he can't let this woman go. If that spreads through our circles, his reputation will suffer.” “Don't worry.” Huang struck his chest. “If Uncle Four asks, I'll take full responsibility.” On the surface, Huang was proving such a good friend that refusing his advice would make Chen seem foolishly ungrateful. Chen was shrewd enough to answer with apparent pleasure. “With you helping me like this, what more could I ask? I'll attend to it tomorrow.” This was merely to put him off. Chen had no intention of following the advice. Reflecting alone, he felt that he had asked Huang for help only to gain more trouble, with additional complications he had never needed. Thoroughly unhappy, he went to bed early.
